query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) reinforcement to a W-Cu metal-matrix composite can increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.conditions: High-temperature and high-energy neutron irradiation environments
generation.mechanism: The refractory HEA reinforcement can improve thermal conductivity by reducing the thermal boundary resistance between the W and Cu phases, while its high entropy and lattice distortion can enhance mechanical durability and irradiation resistance by reducing defect formation and increasing dislocation mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased thermal conductivity and retained mechanical durability and irradiation resistance
generation.boundary: High-temperature and high-energy neutron irradiation environments
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition and microstructure of the refractory HEA reinforcement, as well as its interfacial properties with the W and Cu phases, are uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate W-Cu metal-matrix composites with and without refractory HEA reinforcement, and subject them to high-temperature and high-energy neutron irradiation environments.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal conductivity of the unreinforced W-Cu metal-matrix composite is higher than that of the reinforced composite, or if the mechanical durability and irradiation resistance of the unreinforced composite are better than those of the reinforced composite, then the hypothesis is falsified.

However, two major weaknesses limited its applications due to the poor ductility at ambient temperature and low strength at high temperature []. Preparing materials into composites is one of the effective ways to improve the properties of materials. A great many of efforts, such as ceramic reinforcement [,] and oxide-dispersion strengthening (ODS) [,,] have been offered to overcome these limitations. () showed how Ni-based FCC HEAs lead to less radiation-induced segregation and fewer voids, although hardness was observed to increase after irradiation. Other studies show results in the same direction, with HEAs improving radiation tolerance in both FCC and BCC structures (). Very recently, W-based quinary HEAs with diverse composition have been synthesized as potential materials for fusion applications. The authors observed the formation of Ti carbides and laves phases at large W concentrations. The authors studied the mechanical response, showing that these materials could lead to twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening (). However, refractory HEAs have never been tested under irradiation for potential uses as PFMs or structural materials in nuclear fusion environments. The main requirements for a suitable reactor wall material are good thermal conductivity, high resistance to sputtering, erosion and neutron irradiation, and the ability to withstand variations in the temperature and magnetic field. The WMoNbTaV alloy can respond to the majority of these demands. The crystalline structure of the alloy is affected by multiple strengthening effects and secondary phases, generating exceptional hardness and mechanical durability []. Ideally, one feature of an appropriate wall material would also be the lack of hydrogen trapping defects created under irradiation, leading to low retention of fusion fuel. In this study, we quantify the amount of retained hydrogen and deuterium in WMoTaNbV and compare results with those of W, the current material of choice. Deuterium is used to model tritium retention properties in order to avoid radiological hazards. Despite the differences in the masses of these hydrogen isotopes, their chemical properties are similar, and their trapping behavior in metals is comparable.
